# Hardware, Memory, and Isolation — Notes

## Core realization

Computer systems are built as layers of abstraction.

Higher layers create concepts that lower layers do not intrinsically understand.

Examples:

```text
C sees variables.

malloc sees allocation chunks.

virtual memory sees pages.

CPU caches see cache lines.

cache coherence sees ownership of cache lines.

the kernel sees processes, credentials, namespaces, and objects.

hardware sees privilege, mappings, permissions, instructions, and addresses.
```

A recurring source of surprising behavior is:

> Different layers divide reality at different boundaries.

---

# Cache coherence

Multiple CPU cores may each cache copies of the same memory.

Example:

```text
Core 0 cache       Core 1 cache

x = 42             x = 42
Shared             Shared
```

Reads can safely occur from both copies.

Writes require stronger coordination.

A coherence protocol such as MESI tracks line states:

```text
M = Modified
E = Exclusive
S = Shared
I = Invalid
```

A core wanting to modify a cache line must obtain appropriate ownership.

Very roughly:

```text
Core 0:
"I need write ownership"

        ↓

other cached copies become invalid

        ↓

Core 0 may modify the line
```

This is part of what allows an instruction such as:

```asm
lock cmpxchg
```

to remain atomic across multiple cores.

---

# Cache lines

Cache coherence generally works on **cache lines**, not individual C variables.

On the x86 machine tested, the relevant line size was 64 bytes.

Example:

```text
64-byte cache line

┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ a │ b │ other nearby data ...               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

The hardware does not inherently know:

```text
a belongs to Thread A
b belongs to Thread B
```

It knows:

```text
these bytes occupy the same coherence unit
```

---

# False sharing

False sharing occurs when two threads modify different variables that happen to reside on the same cache line.

Logically:

```text
Thread A → a
Thread B → b
```

No variable is actually shared.

But hardware sees:

```text
Thread A → cache line X
Thread B → cache line X
```

Each writer repeatedly needs ownership of the same line.

The line therefore ping-pongs between cores.

---

## Experiment

Two adjacent atomics:

```c
typedef struct {
    _Alignas(64) atomic_long a;
    atomic_long b;
} false_shared_pair;
```

Possible layout:

```text
a @ ...9100
b @ ...9108
```

Only 8 bytes apart, therefore likely on the same 64-byte line.

Separate them:

```c
typedef struct {
    _Alignas(64) atomic_long a;
    _Alignas(64) atomic_long b;
} separated_pair;
```

Possible layout:

```text
a @ ...9080
b @ ...90c0
```

64 bytes apart.

Measured result from the experiment:

```text
same atomic        ≈ 1.695 s
false sharing      ≈ 1.893 s
separate lines     ≈ 0.186 s
```

The striking comparison is:

```text
false sharing
vs
separate cache lines
```

because the C-level workload is almost identical.

The memory layout alone produced an enormous performance difference.

---

# Why false sharing exists

False sharing is not simply a forgotten engineering mistake.

Cache lines are a compromise.

Larger cache lines provide:

- good spatial locality;
- fewer tags;
- less coherence metadata;
- efficient bulk memory transfers.

But they increase:

- false sharing;
- unnecessary data transfer;
- coherence traffic when nearby data is independently modified.

Smaller lines reduce false sharing but require much more bookkeeping.

Therefore the design assumes:

> Nearby memory is often accessed together.

Usually that assumption is beneficial.

False sharing is a case where the assumption fails.

---

# Safety vs performance

False sharing normally does NOT break correctness.

The cache-coherence protocol still preserves the correct memory values.

Instead:

```text
Safety:
preserved

Performance:
degraded badly
```

This is an important systems distinction.

A mechanism can preserve the invariant while becoming practically unusable.

---

# Memory isolation is not allocator bookkeeping

`malloc()` maintains allocator metadata:

```text
this chunk is free
this chunk is allocated
this chunk has size N
```

But the CPU does not consult `malloc()` before every pointer access.

If code constructs a bad pointer that still lands on another valid mapping inside the same process, the CPU may permit that access.

That is one reason memory corruption bugs exist.

The stronger process isolation boundary comes from:

```text
virtual memory
+
page tables
+
MMU enforcement
```

---

# Virtual addresses are not physical addresses

Two processes can use the same numerical virtual address while referring to unrelated RAM.

Example:

```text
Process A                      Process B

virtual 0x7000                 virtual 0x7000
      │                              │
      ▼                              ▼
A page tables                  B page tables
      │                              │
      ▼                              ▼
physical page X                physical page Y
```

Therefore:

```text
same virtual address
```

does not imply:

```text
same physical memory
```

The meaning of a virtual address depends on the active address-space mapping.

---

# The MMU as enforcement

For each memory access, the hardware effectively evaluates something like:

```text
current page tables
+
virtual address
+
requested operation
+
current privilege level
        ↓
is this access permitted?
```

Possible outcomes include:

```text
mapped + permitted
    → perform access

unmapped
    → page fault

mapped but forbidden
    → page fault
```

This is much stronger than software convention.

The CPU itself prevents the forbidden architectural access from completing.

---

# Page faults are not always errors

A page fault may mean:

```text
invalid access
```

but it may also represent normal operating-system machinery.

Examples:

```text
demand paging
copy-on-write
lazy allocation
```

The CPU traps into the kernel.

The kernel examines the reason and either:

```text
repair mapping + resume instruction
```

or:

```text
deliver failure such as SIGSEGV
```

---

# UIDs are not hardware concepts

The MMU does not know what:

```text
UID 1000
```

means.

UIDs are kernel-level abstractions.

When a process asks:

```c
open("/some/file", ...);
```

the kernel considers things such as:

```text
process credentials
file ownership
permissions
namespaces
capabilities
security policy
```

and decides whether the request is authorized.

Therefore multiple enforcement layers exist:

```text
allocator:
which chunks belong to this allocator?

virtual memory:
which virtual pages exist?

MMU:
may this load/store/execute occur?

kernel authorization:
may this identity request this resource?

CPU privilege:
may this execution context perform this privileged action?
```

---

# Names are not authority

Knowing another process's virtual address is not enough to access its memory.

An address is essentially a **name**.

It is not automatically a **capability**.

Example:

```text
Process A secret:
virtual address 0x7fff12345000
```

Process B knowing that number does not make B's page table map that address to A's physical page.

This is an important security distinction:

> Knowledge of an identifier does not necessarily grant authority over the referenced object.

---

# Threads vs processes

Threads inside one process generally share the same virtual address space.

Therefore the MMU normally does NOT know:

```text
this variable belongs to Thread A
that data structure belongs to Thread B
```

If both threads have access to writable process memory, both can issue loads and stores to it.

Concurrency ownership is therefore largely a software-level invariant.

The CPU provides mechanisms such as:

```text
atomic operations
cache coherence
memory ordering
```

but software creates rules such as:

```text
only the thread holding mutex X may manipulate object Y
```

The hardware does not infer that rule.

---

# Hardware gives mechanisms; software creates meaning

The stack can be viewed as:

```text
transistors
    ↓
cache coherence
    ↓
atomic instructions
    ↓
locks / semaphores
    ↓
data structures
    ↓
transactions
    ↓
application invariants
```

Each layer depends on guarantees provided by the layer below.

The lower layer generally does not understand the higher-level purpose.

Example:

```text
CMPXCHG does not know it is implementing a lock.

The lock does not know it protects a linked list.

The linked list does not know it represents a job queue.

The job queue does not know what application-level failure means.
```

Correctness emerges from composing these guarantees correctly.

---

# Spectre / Meltdown lesson

Architectural permission checks may remain correct while microarchitectural state leaks information.

Conceptually:

```text
architectural state:
access denied

microarchitectural state:
cache affected by transient execution
```

This reveals a critical security principle:

> A state transition assumed to be unobservable may still leave observable side effects at another layer.

The isolation invariant can therefore fail even when the architectural model appears intact.

---

# Containers

Containers feel like separate machines:

```text
my filesystem
my processes
my network
my users
my memory
```

But ordinary Linux containers usually share the host kernel.

Their isolation is assembled from mechanisms such as:

```text
PID namespaces
mount namespaces
network namespaces
IPC namespaces
user namespaces
cgroups
capabilities
seccomp
LSMs
page tables
MMU protection
```

Therefore:

> Container isolation is not one mechanism.

It is a property created by the composition of many mechanisms.

---

# Container authorization is contextual

A decision may depend on multiple pieces of state:

```text
Which process made the request?

Which namespace is it in?

What UID does that identity map to?

Which capabilities are present?

Which mount namespace is active?

Which object is being accessed?

What permissions does that object have?

Does security policy permit the operation?
```

So authorization may conceptually resemble:

```text
Allowed =
f(credentials,
  namespaces,
  capabilities,
  object state,
  mappings,
  policy,
  requested operation)
```

All of that state must remain coherent enough for the decision to mean what the kernel believes it means.

---

# Trusted Computing Base

A useful concept is the **Trusted Computing Base (TCB)**.

The TCB is roughly:

> The collection of mechanisms whose correctness must be trusted for the security property to hold.

For a container executing hostile code, a large portion of the shared host kernel becomes relevant to the isolation boundary.

Therefore:

```text
container security guarantee
        depends on
relevant host-kernel behavior remaining correct
```

A kernel privilege-escalation bug can undermine the component responsible for maintaining the isolation itself.

---

# Trust boundaries

A **trust boundary** is not necessarily physical.

It is a point where:

> Data or control moves from something whose behavior is assumed into something that must be independently constrained or verified.

Examples:

```text
userspace → kernel
container → shared kernel
guest VM → hypervisor
network peer → local service
thread → synchronized shared object
```

---

# Containers vs VMs

A normal container looks approximately like:

```text
container A userspace
container B userspace
        ↓
========================
shared host kernel
========================
        ↓
hardware
```

A VM introduces another isolation layer:

```text
guest application
        ↓
guest kernel
        ↓
guest page tables
        ↓
guest "physical" memory
        ↓
========================
hypervisor-controlled translation
========================
        ↓
actual host physical memory
```

The guest kernel can believe it owns a physical page.

But its "physical address" is itself translated before reaching actual host RAM.

Therefore compromising the guest kernel does not automatically grant control over the host's physical mappings.

The critical assumption has moved.

---

# MicroVMs

MicroVMs try to retain relatively lightweight deployment while moving the isolation boundary toward virtualization hardware / VMMs.

The conceptual change is not:

> bugs disappear

but:

> the shared trust relationship changes.

Instead of trusting the entire general-purpose host kernel as the sole boundary around hostile code, the system attempts to rely on a smaller virtualization boundary.

This is an example of:

**TCB minimization**

---

# Isolation is constructed, not inherent

A process boundary is not a plastic wall around RAM.

A container namespace is not a separate physical machine.

A UID is not physically stamped onto memory.

A virtual machine's guest physical address is not necessarily actual physical RAM.

These are constructed relationships maintained through:

```text
metadata
mappings
permissions
privilege levels
synchronization
kernel logic
hardware enforcement
```

The abstraction becomes real only because the relevant mechanisms continually preserve its invariant.

---

# Recurring systems pattern

Different layers partition reality differently:

```text
C object
allocator chunk
virtual page
physical page
cache line
process
namespace
container
VM
```

A higher layer often assumes that a lower-level boundary matches its conceptual boundary.

Bugs and performance pathologies appear when that assumption is wrong.

Examples:

```text
false sharing:
C objects differ, cache-line boundary does not

Dirty COW:
logical copy-on-write invariant violated by interleaving

Spectre:
architectural permission boundary does not fully contain microarchitectural observation

container escape:
high-level namespace/isolation property fails because lower-level kernel enforcement is compromised
```

---

# General systems-security lesson

For every abstraction ask:

### Invariant
What must remain true?

### Mechanism
What lower-level mechanism is supposed to preserve it?

### Assumptions
What must other components do correctly?

### Failure
What happens when one assumption becomes false?

### Detection
Can the system tell that the assumption failed?

### Containment
Does the failure remain local?

### Recovery
Can the system return to a valid state?

### Adversarial angle
Can someone intentionally force the bad state or timing?

### Evidence
What observation actually justifies believing the invariant holds?

### Uncertainty
What can the system not know from its available observations?

### Lesson
How should the next design change?

---

# Working thesis

> Correctness is correctness under assumptions.

And a useful extension:

> Abstraction is the art of turning lower-level guarantees into stronger higher-level contracts without accidentally assuming guarantees the lower layer never provided.

Hardware supplies relatively small, strong primitives.

Software composes them into much richer concepts.

The flexibility of that design is what makes modern systems powerful.

It is also what makes failures at abstraction boundaries so interesting.

These two should make a decent starting pair for the learning repo: something like 01_concurrency_and_ordering.md and 02_memory_isolation_and_abstraction.md.

Yes — immutability changes the problem dramatically, because most of the nasty synchronization problem comes from this possibility:

“The state I am reading may change while I am reasoning about it.”

If an object genuinely cannot change after creation, then concurrent readers basically stop conflicting with each other.

The problem shifts from “who may touch this state right now?” to “which version of the state should I be looking at?”

That is a huge change.

Consider the mutable case:

C
struct Account {
    long balance;
    long withdrawals;
};

Thread A might do:

C
account.balance -= 10;
account.withdrawals += 10;

while B reads it.

Without synchronization B might observe:

balance     = 90
withdrawals = 0

even though the intended invariant is:

balance + withdrawals == 100

So we need a mutex or some other mechanism because the object can exist temporarily in an intermediate state.

With an immutable representation, we can instead construct:

old Account:
    balance = 100
    withdrawals = 0

new Account:
    balance = 90
    withdrawals = 10

and never modify the old one.

Then the operation becomes:

construct complete new state
        ↓
publish new state

A reader sees either:

OLD

or:

NEW

but doesn't have to observe the object being assembled halfway.

That gives us a really important transformation:

MUTABLE SHARED STATE

      object
        ▲
       / \
      /   \
 reader   writer
           │
     modifies in place

Problem:
"What is happening while I read?"

versus:

IMMUTABLE STATE

 old object     new object
      ▲              ▲
      │              │
    readers       constructed
                    privately
                       │
                       ▼
                publish reference

Problem:
"Which version am I reading?"

Notice that synchronization hasn't disappeared.

It has moved.

The contested thing becomes the reference

Suppose:

C
struct Config {
    int x;
    int y;
};

Instead of everybody mutating one object, imagine:

C
_Atomic(struct Config *)current;

A writer conceptually does:

C
struct Config *next = malloc(sizeof(*next));

next->x = 10;
next->y = 20;

/* object is now complete */

atomic_store(&current, next);

Readers do:

C
struct Config *snapshot = atomic_load(&current);

printf("%d %d\n", snapshot->x, snapshot->y);

Now the large structure itself doesn't need to be atomically rewritten.

Only this tiny transition does:

current:
OLD_POINTER → NEW_POINTER

That's the same trick we saw with the spinlock!

Use one tiny atomic state transition to establish a much larger property.

atomic pointer publication
          ↓
selects one complete immutable object
          ↓
readers safely inspect arbitrarily large state

This pattern appears everywhere.

There are really three increasingly pleasant cases.

Mutable shared object
A reads/writes X
B reads/writes X

You need careful synchronization around X.

Immutable object, mutable pointer
A reads immutable version X
B creates immutable version Y
atomic pointer: X → Y

Now synchronization is concentrated around publication/version selection.

Completely immutable object with fixed lifetime
object created
object safely published
everybody only reads forever

After publication, readers may require essentially no synchronization at all for the contents.

This is why immutable data structures are so attractive in concurrent programming.

And it connects directly to cache coherence.

Remember false sharing?

Two writers caused:

Core A wants cache line
Core B wants cache line
Core A wants cache line
Core B wants cache line
...

because writes require ownership changes.

But if everybody only reads:

Core A: Shared
Core B: Shared
Core C: Shared
Core D: Shared

that's the cache's happy place.

Nobody needs to invalidate everybody else's copy.

So immutability doesn't merely simplify reasoning.

It can make the hardware coherence problem much easier too:

many readers
     +
no writers
     =
very little ownership fighting
But immutability doesn't eliminate concurrency problems

This is where it gets interesting.

Suppose everyone has an immutable object.

We still have to answer:

How did the reader obtain its pointer?

If a writer does:

C
current = new_config;

at the wrong time or without appropriate synchronization, another thread might theoretically observe the pointer without being entitled to assume all of the object's initialization is visible.

This is where safe publication, acquire, release, and happens-before become important.

Conceptually we want:

Writer:

write x
write y
write z
     ↓
PUBLISH POINTER
══════════════════ synchronization
READ POINTER
     ↓
Reader may now infer:
x/y/z initialization happened before my reads

This is probably the cleanest motivation we've encountered yet for learning acquire/release memory ordering.

We don't just need:

“The pointer update itself isn't torn.”

We need:

“If I see the new pointer, I must also see the state that was constructed before it was published.”

Much deeper guarantee.

And there's another nasty problem:

When can we free the old immutable object?

Suppose:

Reader A obtains pointer to OLD

Writer B publishes NEW

Writer B:
"OLD isn't current anymore, free it!"

But A is still reading OLD.

Boom:

use-after-free

So immutability solved:

concurrent modification

but introduced/emphasized:

lifetime management

The question becomes:

How do I know that nobody could still be holding the old version?

That leads into some very interesting systems techniques:

reference counting
hazard pointers
epochs
RCU (Read-Copy-Update)
garbage collection

RCU in particular is almost exactly the philosophy we're discussing:

READ
    readers cheaply access existing immutable-ish state

COPY
    writer makes a modified copy

UPDATE
    atomically publish new version

WAIT
    ensure old readers are gone

RECLAIM
    free old version

Linux uses RCU extensively because kernels have lots of situations with:

many readers
few writers
read performance extremely important

That will be a fantastic topic later.

Another subtlety for C specifically:

C
const struct Config *p;

does not necessarily mean the underlying object is genuinely immutable.

It mostly means:

“You may not modify this object through this particular pointer.”

Another alias might still have:

C
struct Config *q;

and modify the same storage.

So:

C
const

is useful but isn't automatically an ownership/isolation system.

True immutability is often a design invariant, not something C completely enforces for you.

You can strengthen it with things like read-only memory mappings, APIs that hide writable aliases, ownership discipline, etc.

There's also a distributed-systems connection that I think you'll like.

Mutable state asks:

“What is the current value right now?”

Immutable/versioned state lets us instead say:

Version 17 = X
Version 18 = Y
Version 19 = Z

Now disagreement becomes:

Node A has version 18
Node B has version 19

rather than:

“Somebody changed the same object underneath me.”

That is conceptually much easier to reason about.

Git is basically an extreme example of this philosophy:

commit A
   ↓
commit B
   ↓
commit C

Old states don't mutate.

New states refer to prior ones.

A lot of distributed systems use similar ideas:

append-only logs
immutable events
MVCC database versions
content-addressed objects
Merkle trees
event sourcing

because immutability turns:

"Who changed reality while I wasn't looking?"

into:

"Which version of reality do I currently know about?"

The second problem is still hard, but it is often much more tractable.

So I think the most compact way to summarize the difference is:

Mutability makes synchronization about controlling concurrent changes to state.

Immutability makes synchronization primarily about publishing, selecting, ordering, and eventually reclaiming versions of state.

It doesn't eliminate shared-state problems.

It moves the dangerous transition into a much smaller place.

And that is very much the same systems-design pattern we've been seeing repeatedly:

Reduce the amount of state whose correctness depends on synchronization.

That is one of the strongest tools you have for making concurrent systems easier to reason about.

Yes — your first connection makes sense, but I’d sharpen it slightly: what you were dealing with was less “mutability used for concurrency” and more mutable state being used to encode a protocol/state machine. Concurrency becomes one possible way that protocol can be violated.

1. Your camera API was basically a state machine with ownership and lifetime rules

From your description, the camera was not just “an object with some mutable fields.” It had legal and illegal states.

Conceptually, something like:

CLOSED
  │
  │ get/open handle
  ▼
OPEN
  │
  │ configure
  ▼
CONFIGURED
  │
  │ begin acquisition
  ▼
ACQUIRING

And the legality of operations depended on the current state:

OPEN:
    node map writable
    exposure writable
    focus mode writable

ACQUIRING:
    some node-map operations forbidden

AUTO FOCUS ENABLED:
    manually controlled focus-related parameters become read-only

That is exactly the kind of thing we're studying.

The invariant might have been:

There is at most one valid system handle, and camera operations occur only when the device is in a state that permits them.

The mutable state is what records:

system handle exists
camera initialized
acquisition running
focus mode = automatic

and that state determines which transitions are legal.

So this:

C
set_auto_focus(true);
set_manual_focus(42);

isn't necessarily a race. Even in a single thread it could be an invalid state transition:

MANUAL_CONTROL_ALLOWED
        ↓
enable auto
        ↓
MANUAL_CONTROL_FORBIDDEN
        ↓
attempt manual control
        ↓
FAULT

That's very close to a concept called typestate, except typestate systems try to make the legal operations depend explicitly on the object's state, sometimes even at compile time.

Your vendor API sounds like it was enforcing much of it dynamically.

And the singleton handle introduces another invariant:

number_of_system_handles ≤ 1

So if this happens:

MATLAB call A:
getSystemHandle()
→ handle exists

MATLAB call B:
getSystemHandle()
→ attempts second initialization

the API can end up violating an assumption that its own internal state machine depends upon.

Your persistent session object was effectively solving a lifetime problem:

MATLAB function invocation ends

BUT

camera session lifetime must continue

so instead of:

call → initialize everything → perform operation → destroy everything

you built:

call 1:
create session
        ↓
persistent state

call 2:
reuse session
        ↓

call 3:
reuse session
        ↓

eventually:
explicitly destroy session

That's absolutely related to what we've been discussing about pointers and lifetime.

The session object became a little authority token:

If I possess this valid session object, I have access to the persistent underlying camera state.

And then its correctness depends on things like:

session still valid
underlying handle still exists
device is in compatible state
operation is legal in current mode
nobody else has invalidated the assumptions

If multiple MATLAB calls/threads could enter concurrently, then all of that state becomes a shared mutable concurrency problem too.

But even without concurrency, it's already a protocol correctness problem.

That's an important distinction:

Mutability creates temporal rules even with only one thread.

Concurrency makes those temporal rules much harder because several actors can change the state between your observation and your action.

That is almost a textbook TOCTOU pattern:

C
if (camera_is_not_acquiring()) {
    /* assumption: node map is writable */

    modify_node_map();
}

If another thread can start acquisition between those operations:

A: checks NOT ACQUIRING
B: starts acquisition
A: modifies node map

then your previously valid state assumption has expired.

So your camera API is actually a great future case study because it combines:

persistent lifetime
singleton ownership
mutable state
state-dependent permissions
invalid transitions
potential concurrency
external physical hardware

which is much richer than our toy counters.

2. Large state absolutely can become a cache-coherence problem

Your instinct here is also right.

A pointer is tiny:

C
struct HugeState *current;

but the object might be:

4 KB
1 MB
100 MB

and therefore span:

many many cache lines

Cache coherence doesn't somehow make the whole object one unit.

If an object is 4096 bytes and the machine has 64-byte cache lines:

4096 / 64 = 64 cache lines

Hardware treats those 64 lines independently.

So this:

HugeObject
┌──────┬──────┬──────┬──────┬───── ... ─────┐
│ L0   │ L1   │ L2   │ L3   │               │
└──────┴──────┴──────┴──────┴────────────────┘

can have different cache-line ownership situations simultaneously.

Core A could effectively own:

L0, L1, L2

while Core B owns:

L20, L21

without a problem.

The painful case is when both repeatedly write the same lines.

So large state isn't inherently bad.

The important question becomes:

How is access distributed spatially across that state?

If:

Thread A writes first half
Thread B writes second half

and the boundary is cleanly separated across cache lines, that can scale nicely.

If:

Thread A touches bytes throughout object
Thread B touches bytes throughout object

you may get coherence traffic all over the place.

And this is where immutable snapshots become surprisingly powerful.

Suppose you have:

C
_Atomic(struct State *)current;

and State is enormous.

A writer builds:

State B

privately while readers continue using:

State A

Then eventually you perform one tiny publication:

current:
A → B

The pointer is indeed a tiny toehold.

But that's exactly why it's useful.

You're taking a huge amount of state:

megabytes of configuration
trees
tables
indexes
metadata

and reducing the contested transition to:

8-byte pointer changes from X to Y

The larger object doesn't need to move atomically.

It only needs to be complete before publication and stable afterward.

Conceptually:

Writer                              Readers

build B privately

B.line0
B.line1
B.line2
...
B.line1000

       atomic publish
A ─────────────────────→ B
                         │
                         ▼
                  future readers
                  choose B

Readers already holding A may continue reading A.

That's not brittle at all if lifetime is handled properly. It is one of the most powerful patterns in systems programming.

The tiny pointer is basically acting like a commit record:

Everything reachable through this pointer is now the committed version.

That's remarkably similar to what databases and distributed systems do with much larger state.

There is still a cost.

If State is 100 MB and every update requires copying 100 MB:

immutable snapshot design
→ terrible

So real systems often use structural sharing.

Instead of:

OLD TREE
     ↓
copy entire tree
     ↓
NEW TREE

you might copy only the path that changed:

                old root
               /        \
              A          B
            /   \       / \
           C     D     E   F


modify D


                new root
               /        \
          new A           B  ← shared
          /   \
         C    new D
         ↑
       shared

Most of the old structure remains shared because it's immutable.

Only changed pieces are recreated.

That's the basis of a lot of persistent/functional data structures.

You can apply the same idea more crudely in systems code with:

chunks
pages
sub-objects
copy-on-write
per-component versioning

instead of copying gigantic monolithic objects.

So there's an interesting spectrum:

one giant mutable object
    → lots of synchronization complexity

one giant immutable snapshot
    → simple reasoning, potentially huge copy cost

immutable substructures + structural sharing
    → more design complexity, much less copying

sharded mutable state
    → independent ownership, reduced contention

And cache lines sit underneath all of them.

What I think ties both of your questions together is granularity.

Your camera API had a granularity problem around state:

When does the camera become "acquiring"?

Which settings become invalid together?

What lifetime does the system handle have?

Our cache experiment had a granularity problem around hardware:

C says:
a and b are separate

hardware says:
a and b occupy one coherence unit

Immutable publication has another granularity choice:

What counts as one version?

whole application?
one tree?
one page?
one object?
one configuration record?

A huge amount of systems design is really:

Choose the smallest useful unit over which an invariant has to be maintained.

Too large, and everything contends or gets copied.

Too small, and coordinating the pieces becomes complicated.

That is why the pointer trick is so powerful: it lets the decision about which version is current be tiny even when the state selected by that decision is enormous.

Yes — but only partly, and the distinction is really revealing.

The biggest correction first: mxCalloc did not fix this because it “forced contiguous blocks.” malloc, mxMalloc, and mxCalloc all give you a logically contiguous range of virtual addresses for the requested object. calloc's defining difference is that the allocated bytes are zero-initialized; mxCalloc also puts the allocation under MATLAB's memory-management conventions.

So if changing only the allocator changed:

free → corruption / access violation / even BSOD

into:

mxFree → clean shutdown

then something deeper was probably being exposed or masked.

And the things we've just been discussing give us a much better vocabulary for what could have been happening.

Your camera system had at least three overlapping lifetime domains

Something approximately like:

MATLAB lifetime
    │
    ├── mxArray objects
    ├── MATLAB allocator
    └── MEX invocation/session lifetime

MEX C/C++ lifetime
    │
    ├── native pointers
    ├── persistent session object
    └── buffers

camera SDK lifetime
    │
    ├── system handle
    ├── camera handle
    ├── acquisition state
    └── buffers possibly still referenced by SDK/driver

kernel/driver lifetime
    │
    └── DMA / device I/O / mapped memory

Now imagine you allocate:

C
buffer = malloc(...);

give buffer to the camera SDK, MATLAB processes the resulting image, and later do:

C
free(buffer);

Your C code may believe:

“I am finished with this allocation.”

But the camera subsystem may still believe:

“This buffer remains valid for acquisition / callback / DMA.”

Then free() doesn't itself create the bug.

It merely makes an existing lifetime violation become observable:

camera still holds pointer P
        ↓
program frees P
        ↓
allocator reuses/changes P's storage
        ↓
camera/driver writes through stale P
        ↓
unrelated memory is corrupted

That's classic use-after-free, except the actor holding the stale reference could be hardware/driver/API state rather than another C function.

And that would fit your memory of seeing what looked like camera data where stack/control state should have been.

The BSOD detail makes the situation more suspicious

A normal bad userspace pointer should generally kill MATLAB/the MEX process with an access violation.

It should not normally BSOD Windows.

A blue screen means the kernel detected a fatal kernel-mode failure.

Since a physical camera typically involves a kernel driver, one plausible architecture is:

MATLAB
  ↓
MEX
  ↓
vendor userspace SDK
  ↓
vendor kernel driver
  ↓
camera

So if malformed buffer ownership or lifetime caused the kernel-side driver to scribble somewhere it shouldn't, a BSOD becomes much more plausible.

That doesn't prove the camera vendor had a vulnerability. There are several possibilities:

your code violated SDK lifetime requirements

allocator/deallocator families were mixed

wrong buffer size/alignment was supplied

SDK retained a pointer longer than expected

MATLAB moved/destroyed something you assumed persisted

vendor SDK had a userspace bug

vendor kernel driver mishandled a buffer

some combination of the above

But user-controlled camera bytes overwriting control state is absolutely a memory-corruption symptom, not normal behavior.

If you literally saw ESP overwritten with recognizable image/camera data, that strongly suggests some buffer overrun, stale pointer, wrong size, or equivalent corruption somewhere in the chain.

Why could mxCalloc apparently fix it?

Several possibilities.

The most obvious is zero initialization.

Compare:

C
p = mxMalloc(size);

with:

C
p = mxCalloc(count, size);

The latter starts as:

00 00 00 00 00 00 ...

Suppose some SDK structure contained fields you were expected to initialize:

C
struct BufferInfo {
    void *data;
    size_t size;
    int flags;
    void *callback;
};

If some field accidentally remained uninitialized with malloc:

flags    = 0x6ab3912f
callback = 0xf17382...

but happened to become:

flags    = 0
callback = NULL

with calloc, the apparent problem could disappear.

That would be a Heisenbug-like masking effect, not proof that calloc was intrinsically the right synchronization mechanism.

Another possibility is allocator-family consistency.

If you had something resembling:

C
p = malloc(...);
...
mxFree(p);       // bad pairing

or:

C
p = mxMalloc(...);
...
free(p);         // potentially bad

then you're violating the allocator's ownership contract.

The safe conceptual pairing is:

malloc/calloc/realloc  ↔ free

mxMalloc/mxCalloc/...  ↔ mxFree

because the allocator that created an object is generally the allocator whose metadata knows how to destroy it.

That's another instance of:

Possessing the pointer is not sufficient knowledge to know how its storage may be reclaimed.

Very much the theme we've been discussing.

And here's where your second question does connect, but not through cache coherence specifically.

The shared principle is:

Memory layout and memory lifetime are properties of a lower layer that higher-level code can accidentally make assumptions about.

Our false-sharing experiment was:

C sees:
a and b are independent

hardware sees:
same cache line

Your camera issue may have been closer to:

MEX code sees:
this pointer is no longer needed

camera SDK sees:
this buffer is still registered

allocator sees:
this region can now be reused

driver sees:
write incoming frame here

Every participant can have a locally reasonable interpretation while the combined system has incompatible beliefs about the same memory.

That is extremely close to the systems theme we're pursuing.

But I wouldn't connect it like:

calloc fixed cache-line contention

because there's no reason to think that.

I'd connect it like:

false sharing
    → disagreement about memory granularity

camera corruption
    → probable disagreement about memory ownership/lifetime/layout

both
    → higher-level assumptions fail because the lower layer
      partitions/manages memory differently than expected
And physical contiguity is another important distinction

Even if you allocate:

C
char *p = malloc(1024 * 1024);

C gives you a contiguous virtual address range:

p
p+1
p+2
...

That does not require the backing physical pages to be adjacent:

virtual pages:

V0 V1 V2 V3

 ↓  ↓  ↓  ↓

physical:

P91 P14 P802 P35

The MMU makes that scattered physical storage appear contiguous.

For normal CPU code, that's fine.

But hardware devices doing DMA can introduce another layer. Depending on the driver/device/IOMMU design, the driver may need to pin pages, build scatter/gather lists, create DMA mappings, or otherwise tell the device where the real backing storage lives.

So if the camera SDK accepted raw buffers for asynchronous acquisition, you were potentially sitting exactly at the intersection of:

C virtual memory
MATLAB allocator
Windows VM
device driver
DMA mappings
physical camera

That is a much richer problem than “I malloc'd an array.”

And your persistent singleton/session design makes even more sense in retrospect. It was effectively trying to keep all those resources alive under one coherent lifetime:

session exists
    ↓
system handle valid
    ↓
camera handle valid
    ↓
buffers valid
    ↓
acquisition state known

rather than reconstructing and destroying pieces independently across MEX entry points.

So, amusingly, yes: question 2 helps explain why question 1 now feels less mysterious, but the common concept isn't cache lines.

It's ownership granularity + lifetime + hidden lower-level state.

And if you ever still have that old code, this would actually be an amazing specimen for this project. We could reconstruct the ownership graph—who allocates each pointer, who retains it, when the camera is allowed to access it, who frees it—and probably formulate the original bug as an explicit violated invariant even if we can no longer reproduce the BSOD.

Ah — yes, that changes the picture substantially. In that architecture, MATLAB was not retaining or later operating on the camera's raw buffer. The flow was more like:

enter MEX function
    ↓
allocate native camera buffer
    ↓
camera/SDK writes image into native buffer
    ↓
create MATLAB mxArray<double>
    ↓
copy/convert native pixels → MATLAB array
    ↓
free native camera buffer
    ↓
return mxArray to MATLAB

So my previous idea of “MATLAB may still hold the native pointer after you free it” doesn't fit what you actually built.

It also makes your allocator observation more interesting.

The first thing I'd correct is that mxCalloc() did not fix things by making the allocation contiguous. malloc, mxMalloc, and mxCalloc all present you with a contiguous range of virtual addresses for the requested allocation. mxCalloc's important distinguishing property is that the memory starts zeroed:

C
p = mxMalloc(N);       // contents initially unspecified
p = mxCalloc(n, size); // contents initially all zero

So if changing:

C
mxMalloc(...)

to:

C
mxCalloc(...)

made the corruption disappear, my attention would immediately go to a few possibilities.

The most interesting one is something in the native camera path depended accidentally on initially-zero memory.

Imagine the buffer or some adjacent descriptor looked conceptually like:

C
struct Frame {
    void *data;
    size_t bytes;
    int flags;
    void *something;
};

If not every field was explicitly initialized, mxMalloc could leave:

flags     = random old heap bytes
something = random pointer-looking junk

while mxCalloc produces:

flags     = 0
something = NULL

Suddenly the exact same API sequence “works.”

That doesn't mean calloc solved the underlying invariant. It may simply have supplied an assumption that some code was silently relying on:

unspecified fields begin as zero.

That's a wonderfully relevant example for this project.

Another possibility — and given your memory of recognizable camera/image junk corrupting control state, one I'd take seriously — is a buffer size/stride mismatch or overrun.

Suppose you calculated:

C
width * height * bytes_per_pixel

but the camera actually wrote each row using a pitch/stride:

row data + padding
row data + padding
...

or a pixel format needed more bytes than expected.

Then you might allocate:

expected image size
┌────────────────────────────┐
│                            │
└────────────────────────────┘

while the camera writes:

actual camera output
┌────────────────────────────┬──────────────►
│ image data                 │ OVERFLOW
└────────────────────────────┴──────────────►

Changing allocators can alter where that block lands and what surrounds it.

So one allocator layout might produce:

[camera buffer][allocator metadata]
                ↑
                overwritten

and then:

C
mxFree(buffer);

blows up because the allocator's bookkeeping was destroyed.

Another allocation pattern might produce:

[camera buffer][unused/padding/less-sensitive memory]

and suddenly the bug appears to disappear.

That is a classic characteristic of memory corruption:

Changing something apparently unrelated to the bug changes whether the bug manifests.

And calloc also zeroes the allocation, which changes heap contents and sometimes heap behavior enough to expose/mask undefined behavior differently.

There's another especially relevant possibility with cameras: was acquisition completely finished before the buffer was freed?

Even though the allocation and free both happened within one MEX call, you can still have:

MEX thread                     camera / driver

allocate buffer
register buffer ──────────────►

start/read frame

SDK call returns?
                               device/driver still finishing?
copy data

free(buffer)

                               late write ─────► stale pointer

Whether that was possible depends entirely on the vendor API's contract. Some acquisition calls synchronously guarantee the buffer is no longer owned by the device when they return; others involve queued buffers, callbacks, streaming, DMA, etc.

So:

“Allocated and freed within one function”

doesn't necessarily prove:

“Only my function could access the storage during that entire lifetime.”

The meaningful lifetime would instead be:

allocation
    ↓
camera gains right to access
    ↓
camera definitively relinquishes right to access
    ↓
free is legal

Which is exactly the ownership/lifetime distinction we've been discussing.

And the fact that the failure happened on mxFree is especially suggestive.

A heap overrun often doesn't explode at the moment of the bad write.

You can have:

camera writes 500 bytes beyond buffer
        ↓
nothing visibly happens
        ↓
lots of other code executes
        ↓
mxFree(buffer)
        ↓
allocator examines corrupted metadata
        ↓
💥

So the human interpretation becomes:

“mxFree crashed.”

But the true failure may have occurred thousands or millions of instructions earlier.

That's a beautiful example of:

failure occurrence
≠
failure detection

which belongs directly in your framework.

As for the ESP/camera-data observation: if the debugger really showed camera-like bytes having corrupted stack/control information, that strongly points toward memory corruption, but I wouldn't identify exactly which component was responsible without the old code/dump.

Potential causes would include things like:

incorrect buffer dimensions
incorrect stride
incorrect element size
incorrect destination pointer arithmetic
incorrect SDK structure initialization
asynchronous access after free
vendor SDK overflow
driver bug
calling-convention/signature error

Some are your MEX layer, some could be the vendor userspace library, and some potentially the driver.

And a genuine Windows BSOD is significant because normal malformed userspace memory access should ordinarily kill MATLAB, not the whole OS. If it really crossed into a bugcheck, there was likely kernel-mode involvement somewhere in the failure chain — unsurprising for a camera with a driver — but that alone wouldn't establish that the vendor driver itself was defective.

And yes, question 2 kind of answers question 1

Not through cache coherence directly.

The deeper connection is:

Memory has several different granularities and ownership models simultaneously.

Our false-sharing case was:

C programmer:
"a and b are different objects"

CPU coherence:
"a and b happen to be one 64-byte object for my purposes"

Your MEX/camera situation was potentially:

your code:
"these N bytes constitute my image buffer"

allocator:
"these N bytes are one allocation surrounded by my metadata"

camera API:
"I expect a buffer satisfying size/stride/alignment/lifetime condition X"

driver:
"I may have an outstanding operation referring to these pages"

MATLAB:
"I only care about the separate mxArray you eventually return"

The fascinating failure happens when those models almost agree but not quite.

So I wouldn't say:

“The cache-line issue explains the camera crash.”

I'd say:

The cache-line experiment trained you to notice exactly the kind of hidden lower-layer boundary mismatch that could explain why an innocent-looking allocator substitution changed the camera system's behavior.

And your old system would be an unusually good case study if you still have the source. With what you know now, we'd want to reconstruct one very boring-looking table:

object            allocated by    written by       valid until       freed by
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
system handle     vendor API      vendor API       session close     vendor API
camera handle     vendor API      vendor API       camera close      vendor API
raw frame buffer  MEX             camera/SDK+MEX   ???               MEX
MATLAB output     MATLAB/MEX API  MEX/MATLAB       MATLAB lifetime   MATLAB
node map          vendor API      SDK/device       handle lifetime   vendor API

That ??? on the raw buffer is where I'd start.

Because in systems programming, “when am I allowed to free this?” is really “when can I prove that nobody else retains the authority to touch it?”

And that is the same lifetime question that brought us from immutability directly to use-after-free.

That extra detail narrows it a lot, and I think your memory of the old docs may actually have been about wording rather than a different allocation model.

I checked the current MathWorks docs. Today both mxMalloc and mxCalloc explicitly say they allocate contiguous heap space; the meaningful documented difference is that mxCalloc zero-initializes the block while mxMalloc leaves it uninitialized. Both register the allocation with MATLAB’s MEX memory manager, and both can be released with mxFree. 
MathWorks
+2
MathWorks
+2

So if the 2019 docs used looser language for mxMalloc, I would not infer that it meant “possibly noncontiguous physical memory” while mxCalloc guaranteed contiguity. In C/MEX terms, both have to give you a contiguous virtual byte range suitable for pointer arithmetic. MATLAB’s own docs distinguish that from physical RAM; MATLAB arrays are described as contiguous in the process’s address space, not necessarily physically adjacent pages. 
MathWorks
+1

And your pixel-format point is important. If you were correctly unpacking Mono12p, Mono12, Mono8, Mono8p pixel-for-pixel and validating coverage, then the simple hypothesis:

“you just calculated the frame buffer size wrong”

gets considerably weaker.

It doesn't eliminate every memory-corruption possibility, because an SDK could have ancillary metadata, asynchronous ownership, callbacks, or descriptor requirements independent of the pixel payload. But it does mean I would stop treating basic stride/payload arithmetic as the leading explanation.

The really interesting clue becomes this:

mxMalloc  → later mxFree faults / system corruption
mxCalloc  → same algorithm becomes stable

If literally the only semantic change was uninitialized bytes → zeroed bytes, then I would strongly suspect some part of the native path was reading memory that your code thought did not matter yet.

That could be something like:

C
struct CameraThing {
    void *buffer;
    size_t size;
    int flags;
    void *callback;
    int reserved[8];
};

where your code correctly initializes:

C
thing.buffer = p;
thing.size = N;

but the API implicitly expects:

flags = 0
callback = NULL
reserved[] = 0

and either the vendor documentation was unclear or some lower-level implementation incorrectly relied on callers supplying zero-filled storage.

With mxMalloc:

reserved = old heap garbage

With mxCalloc:

reserved = 0

and suddenly the hidden assumption holds.

That kind of bug is especially nasty because the memory allocation call appears to “fix” it while actually changing an initial-state invariant.

And this connects very cleanly to the material we're studying:

The allocation didn't merely give you bytes. It gave you bytes in some initial state.

Your higher-level code may have assumed:

"these bytes are irrelevant until explicitly written"

while another component may effectively have assumed:

"unspecified fields begin at zero"

That is an assumption mismatch.

There is also a second possibility I'd keep alive: the allocator change may have changed heap placement/layout enough to mask an overwrite somewhere else. Heap corruption is notorious for that. A program can decode every pixel perfectly and still scribble one pointer-sized value outside some unrelated native object.

For example:

camera image contents: 100% correct
destination MATLAB image: 100% correct

BUT

some descriptor/callback/cleanup structure
gets overwritten independently

So your validation of the image tells us the image transformation was correct. It doesn't prove all surrounding native memory operations were correct.

The ESP observation is the part I keep coming back to. Recognizable camera bytes appearing in stack/control state is very hard to reconcile with an innocent allocator bookkeeping difference. That sounds much more like:

camera-derived data
        ↓
write reached somewhere it shouldn't
        ↓
control/stack memory corrupted

And if it genuinely produced a Windows bugcheck rather than merely killing MATLAB, then some kernel-mode component was eventually involved. Ordinary bad MEX memory accesses should normally just take out the MATLAB process. A BSOD means the kernel detected something catastrophic, though that still doesn't tell us whether the root cause was your MEX violating an SDK contract or a defect in the vendor driver itself.

The current MEX docs actually reinforce another piece of your recollection: both allocation functions are integrated into MATLAB's automatic cleanup bookkeeping. MATLAB keeps a list of MEX allocations and frees remaining nonpersistent parcels when control returns. MathWorks still recommends explicitly cleaning temporary allocations yourself. 
MathWorks
+2
MathWorks
+2

So the model is roughly:

mxMalloc / mxCalloc
        ↓
ordinary contiguous virtual heap block
        +
MATLAB records ownership of that allocation
        ↓
mxFree removes/deallocates it
or
MATLAB cleans it up at MEX return

That MATLAB registration mechanism is real, but current documentation doesn't indicate different lifetime semantics between mxMalloc and mxCalloc.

Which makes your historical observation more interesting, not less: if one consistently crashed and the other consistently didn't, something was depending on either zero initialization or on an incidental allocator/layout difference.

And that is almost hilariously aligned with what we've just been learning:

same apparent logical operation
different lower-level initial/layout state
        ↓
one execution preserves hidden assumptions
one does not

If you still have that old MEX source someday, I would absolutely revisit it. Not to prove “MATLAB had a vulnerability,” but because with your current mental model we could probably reduce the mystery to a small set of explicit invariants around:

allocation
initialization
SDK ownership
acquisition completion
cleanup

and see exactly which assumption mxCalloc was accidentally satisfying.

Yes — that detail changes the diagnosis quite a bit.

If:

mxMalloc
    + mxFree
    → crash / corruption

mxMalloc
    WITHOUT mxFree
    → works, but leaks

mxCalloc
    + mxFree
    → works and doesn't leak

then the suspicious transition is much more specifically:

the moment you declared that storage dead.

That strongly points toward lifetime/ownership or heap integrity, rather than the allocation itself simply being unusable.

The first possibility I would now take very seriously is that something below your MEX function still had authority to access the buffer when you called mxFree():

MEX                         SDK / driver / camera

allocate P

give P --------------------► retains P somehow

acquire image
process image

mxFree(P)
                            still has P
                                ↓
                            access/write P
                                ↓
                         use-after-free

If you simply remove:

C
mxFree(p);

then p stays allocated.

That is incorrect because it leaks, but it also means:

anybody incorrectly retaining p can continue touching it without immediately hitting reclaimed memory.

That's a classic reason why removing free() can make a memory-corruption bug disappear.

The leak doesn't fix the ownership error. It just prevents the stale pointer from becoming dangerous.

And with a camera, this is more interesting than an ordinary C library because the other actor could potentially be:

vendor userspace SDK
        ↓
kernel driver
        ↓
DMA / device activity

If the API hadn't truly relinquished the buffer before your mxFree, then your MEX thread's idea of:

"I have finished reading this image"

would not necessarily imply:

"Nobody else can access this allocation anymore."

Those are different lifetime claims.

The second major possibility is heap corruption that mxFree() merely detects.

Imagine:

[ allocator metadata ][ your buffer ][ allocator metadata ]

Some bad native write damages:

[ allocator metadatXXXX your buffer ... ]

Everything can appear fine afterward.

Your image can even be pixel-perfect.

Then much later:

C
mxFree(p);

asks the allocator to inspect bookkeeping associated with p.

It discovers nonsense or follows corrupted metadata:

💥

So:

mxFree being where it dies does not necessarily mean mxFree caused the corruption.

It may just be the first code that cares about the corrupted information.

That gives us a distinction that fits your larger study perfectly:

FAULT OCCURS
    ↓
some invalid write

           potentially much later

FAULT DETECTED
    ↓
mxFree examines/reuses damaged state

Those two moments can be very far apart.

And your mxCalloc result is the genuinely strange part.

If the thing being allocated was strictly a raw frame buffer which the camera completely overwrote, then:

mxMalloc → unspecified initial bytes
mxCalloc → zero initial bytes

shouldn't obviously matter to the final frame at all.

That makes me less satisfied with simply saying:

“Something wanted zero initialization.”

That explanation makes sense for a descriptor or structure containing flags/pointers, but much less for a raw image payload that gets filled completely.

So if this really was:

C
unsigned char *raw = mxMalloc(frame_bytes);
camera_get_frame(raw);
...
mxFree(raw);

versus:

C
unsigned char *raw = mxCalloc(frame_bytes, 1);
camera_get_frame(raw);
...
mxFree(raw);

and the latter reliably fixed the crash, then I'd be interested in subtler differences such as:

different heap placement/layout
different surrounding allocator metadata
different reuse of previously freed blocks
different timing
an undocumented SDK assumption
some unrelated undefined behavior being masked

In other words, mxCalloc might not have fixed the underlying problem at all. It may simply have changed memory conditions enough that the failure no longer manifested.

That's extremely common with native memory corruption.

And now your recollection about seeing camera-looking bytes where ESP/stack state should have been becomes more relevant.

Suppose the SDK still had a stale pointer after:

C
mxFree(buffer);

and MATLAB's allocator then reused that region for something else:

before free:

0x12340000 ── camera buffer


after free:

0x12340000 ── available heap storage


later:

0x12340000 ── some MATLAB/native object

Then a delayed camera write to the old address doesn't know anything changed:

camera:
"write frame bytes to 0x12340000"

Physically, those writes still happen to a valid virtual address—but now that address may represent something completely different.

That's the terrifying part of use-after-free:

The pointer can remain numerically correct while its meaning has changed.

That's almost exactly the immutable-pointer/lifetime issue we were discussing earlier.

The address:

0x12340000

doesn't carry:

"I still represent a camera buffer."

That meaning exists only because of an ownership/lifetime invariant.

So I would now express your historical mystery like this:

Invariant: The native frame buffer must remain allocated for every actor capable of accessing it, and it must be freed exactly once after all such access has ended.

Observed failure: Calling mxFree after the apparent frame-processing lifetime caused catastrophic corruption/failure; omitting it prevented the crash but leaked memory.

Strong implication: The program's apparent lifetime for the allocation may not have matched its actual lifetime somewhere in the MEX/SDK/driver chain, or the allocation/heap metadata had already been corrupted and mxFree exposed it.

Mystery: Replacing mxMalloc with mxCalloc changed the manifestation. If this was purely raw fully-overwritten pixel storage, zero initialization alone doesn't provide a satisfying explanation.

And yes — this is now very closely related to the question that brought us here.

You thought the lifetime was:

MEX starts
    ↓
malloc
    ↓
camera read
    ↓
unpack
    ↓
free
    ↓
MEX ends

But the true system lifetime may have been something closer to:

allocate
    ↓
give another subsystem access
    ↓
that subsystem may retain hidden state
    ↓
your code finishes using buffer
    ≠
other subsystem has necessarily relinquished buffer
    ↓
free

That's the same recurring systems lesson:

The local view of state can be completely reasonable while being insufficient to prove the global invariant.

And your “just don't free it” workaround is almost comically illustrative: you preserved safety by refusing to perform reclamation, at the cost of destroying liveness/resource sustainability through an ever-growing leak. That's exactly the kind of tradeoff we're going to keep seeing.

Exactly. The historical diagnosis is probably less valuable now than the fact that you can finally name the classes of failure it belonged to.

Before, the experience was basically:

“This allocator/free pattern crashes, this other one doesn’t, the vendor API has weird state rules, and somehow the MMU/driver gets involved.”

Now you’d approach a similar problem by explicitly separating several questions:

Ownership: who is allowed to touch this object?

Lifetime: when does that right begin and end?

State machine: which operations are legal in which device/software states?

Synchronization: can another actor change the relevant state between check and use?

Granularity: what does each layer consider the unit of protection—object, allocation, page, cache line, handle, device buffer?

Detection: did the bug occur where it crashed, or was the crash merely where corruption was discovered?

Hidden participants: is there a driver, DMA engine, callback, worker thread, allocator, or runtime retaining state that the local function cannot see?

That is already a dramatically better debugging model than “maybe free() is broken.”

And more importantly, it gives you a way to formalize the system before the bug even appears. For a future hardware API, you could literally write down:

Invariant:
A frame buffer is never reclaimed while any subsystem may still access it.

Ownership:
MEX owns allocation.
SDK owns temporary access during acquisition.
Driver/device ownership ends only after operation X guarantees completion.

Legal transitions:
ALLOCATED
→ REGISTERED
→ ACQUIRING
→ COMPLETE
→ UNREGISTERED
→ FREEABLE
→ FREED

Forbidden:
ACQUIRING → FREED
REGISTERED → FREED
FREED → any access

Once you can express the problem like that, debugging becomes much less mystical.

That is really the payoff of what we're doing: not memorizing mutexes, atomics, cache lines, or MMUs independently, but developing a habit of asking:

What state exists, who can observe or mutate it, what transition am I assuming happened, and what mechanism proves that assumption?

Your old camera problem is actually a good example of why this mindset matters. Even if the exact root cause is gone, the shape of the failure is now recognizable.

The cleanest next building block is memory ordering and happens-before, specifically through the very practical problem of publishing state from one thread to another.

You’ve already independently walked right up to it several times:

camera state is initialized
        ↓
some other operation is now allowed

immutable object is constructed
        ↓
publish pointer
        ↓
reader may use object

thread A modifies state
        ↓
hands baton to B
        ↓
B may rely on A's work

So far we've mostly asked:

“Can two threads modify this thing simultaneously?”

The next question is subtler:

“If thread B observes that thread A says it is finished, what is B actually entitled to assume it can see?”

That is the practical reason memory ordering exists.

Suppose we write this:

C
#include <pthread.h>
#include <stdatomic.h>
#include <stdio.h>

int data = 0;
atomic_int ready = 0;

void *producer(void *arg){
    data = 42;
    atomic_store_explicit(&ready, 1, memory_order_relaxed);
    return NULL;
}

void *consumer(void *arg){
    while (atomic_load_explicit(&ready, memory_order_relaxed) == 0) {
    }

    printf("data = %d\n", data);
    return NULL;
}

int main(void){
    pthread_t a, b;

    pthread_create(&a, NULL, producer, NULL);
    pthread_create(&b, NULL, consumer, NULL);

    pthread_join(a, NULL);
    pthread_join(b, NULL);

    return 0;
}

This looks completely reasonable at first glance:

producer:
data = 42
ready = 1

consumer:
wait until ready == 1
read data

Your human reasoning says:

if ready == 1
then obviously data was already set to 42

But memory_order_relaxed does not establish that relationship.

It only promises that accesses to ready itself are atomic.

It doesn't establish:

data = 42
    happens-before
consumer reads data

And because data is ordinary non-atomic memory being accessed across threads without the required synchronization, we're actually back in data-race/undefined-behavior territory.

This is exactly the distinction we were heading toward when we discussed atomics:

Atomicity of one variable is not automatically synchronization of everything around that variable.

Now change two words:

C
void *producer(void *arg){
    data = 42;
    atomic_store_explicit(&ready, 1, memory_order_release);
    return NULL;
}

void *consumer(void *arg){
    while (atomic_load_explicit(&ready, memory_order_acquire) == 0) {
    }

    printf("data = %d\n", data);
    return NULL;
}

Now we've established something much stronger.

The release says conceptually:

Everything I did before publishing ready=1
must be considered complete before this publication.

The acquire says:

If I observe that publication,
everything that happened-before it
is now ordered before my subsequent work.

So we get:

PRODUCER                         CONSUMER

data = 42
    │
    ▼
release store ready = 1
    │
    │ synchronizes-with
    │
    ▼
                         acquire load sees 1
                                │
                                ▼
                         read data

And therefore:

data = 42
    happens-before
read data

That's the guarantee we actually wanted.

This is safe publication

And now look back at our immutable-object example.

Writer:

C
struct Config *next = malloc(sizeof(*next));

next->exposure = 10;
next->gain = 4;
next->width = 1920;
next->height = 1080;

atomic_store_explicit(&current, next, memory_order_release);

Reader:

C
struct Config *snapshot =
    atomic_load_explicit(&current, memory_order_acquire);

printf("%d\n", snapshot->exposure);

The clever bit is that we don't make every member atomic:

exposure
gain
width
height
...

Instead we establish one publication boundary:

construct arbitrary amount of state
               ↓
       RELEASE pointer
══════════════════════════════
       ACQUIRE pointer
               ↓
reader may rely upon everything
that happened before publication

That is the missing machinery behind what we were discussing earlier when I said:

“Build an immutable object privately, then atomically publish the pointer.”

The atomic pointer doesn't merely have to change without tearing.

It has to carry an ordering relationship with it.

And this gives happens-before a much less abstract meaning.

It's not necessarily:

“Event A occurred earlier according to a clock.”

It means something closer to:

The concurrency model gives us sufficient synchronization to prove that A's effects precede B's effects.

That's enormously stronger.

Without synchronization you might physically observe:

A ran at 12:00:00.001
B ran at 12:00:00.002

but that alone isn't the program-level proof we want.

With release/acquire:

A writes state
A release-publishes
B acquire-observes that publication
B reads state

we have a formal ordering relationship.

That is exactly the sort of “what ordering can actually be proven?” question you wanted this project to revolve around.

And relaxed finally has a concrete purpose

memory_order_relaxed is useful when you only care about that atomic object's own value.

Our old counter is perfect:

C
atomic_fetch_add_explicit(&counter, 1, memory_order_relaxed);

If the invariant is merely:

Every increment must be counted exactly once.

we don't necessarily care whether unrelated memory operations are ordered around the counter update.

So relaxed basically says:

“Make this operation atomic, but don't use it as a synchronization event for surrounding state.”

Whereas acquire/release says:

“This atomic operation also carries information about ordering surrounding memory accesses.”

That distinction is huge:

RELAXED

Atomicity:
YES

Cross-object ordering:
essentially no synchronization relationship


RELEASE / ACQUIRE

Atomicity:
YES

Cross-object ordering:
YES, in a specific direction

Then there's:

C
memory_order_seq_cst

which is the strongest/easiest-to-reason-about ordering and adds a single global sequentially consistent order among seq_cst atomic operations.

We can get to its precise meaning after acquire/release clicks.

There is another funny x86 moment waiting for you.

You may compile:

C
atomic_store_explicit(&ready, 1, memory_order_relaxed);

and:

C
atomic_store_explicit(&ready, 1, memory_order_release);

and discover both become something resembling:

asm
mov DWORD PTR [ready], 1

Likewise an acquire load and relaxed load may both become ordinary mov.

And you'll probably go:

WHAT? THEN WHAT DID WE JUST CHANGE?

😄

The answer is that C's memory model and x86's memory model aren't the same thing.

x86 already provides relatively strong ordering guarantees for ordinary loads/stores, so some C ordering requirements require no additional CPU instruction there. The compiler still has to respect the C ordering constraints when moving/optimizing surrounding code.

On a weaker-memory architecture such as ARM, the compiler may need different instructions or barriers.

That will give us another beautiful version of:

C contract
    ↓
compiler
    ↓
ISA contract
    ↓
microarchitecture

which you've already been enjoying with CMPXCHG.

This also leads naturally to TOCTOU

Once acquire/release and happens-before make sense, we can revisit something like:

C
if (camera_state == IDLE){
    modify_node_map();
}

and ask:

What guarantees that camera_state remains IDLE between the check and the operation?

Maybe nothing.

Then:

A: check state == IDLE

B: state = ACQUIRING

A: modify node map

Suddenly the camera API example becomes a concrete TOCTOU exercise instead of an abstract security acronym.

And after that, CAS gives us another possible design:

IDLE → CONFIGURING

as one atomic state transition, so the check and claim become indivisible.

That would tie almost everything we've learned together.

So I think our next little sequence should be:

ready flag with relaxed ordering
        ↓
why atomic ready alone isn't enough
        ↓
release/acquire
        ↓
happens-before
        ↓
safe publication of immutable state
        ↓
compile both to x86 assembly
        ↓
TOCTOU/state-machine experiment

That's the layer I'd do next before going into ABA or serious lock-free data structures. It stays extremely close to the kind of C/C++ state-management problems you've actually encountered, while giving us the formal vocabulary needed for the harder stuff later.

Yes — the memory location is not what makes the value stable. I blurred two separate ideas together there.

The important distinction is:

Correctness comes from synchronization rules. Memory layout mostly entered our discussion because of performance/cache behavior.

Your baton.c counter was deliberately just:

C
long counter = 0;

and that was perfectly fine.

Why? Because the semaphore protocol guaranteed that only one thread could access it at a time:

A has permit
A accesses counter
A posts B
        ↓
B acquires permit
B accesses counter
B posts A

There is no execution like:

A reads counter
B reads counter
A writes counter
B writes counter

because B can't get past:

C
sem_wait(&turn_b);

until A does:

C
sem_post(&turn_b);

So the semaphore is supplying the synchronization.

The counter didn't need to be atomic

This is valid:

C
long counter = 0;

void *worker_a(void *arg){
    sem_wait(&turn_a);
    counter++;
    sem_post(&turn_b);
}

because the shared access is ordered.

Think of it as:

ordinary data
     +
synchronization around access
     =
safe

The same thing happened with the mutex:

C
long counter = 0;

pthread_mutex_lock(&lock);
counter++;
pthread_mutex_unlock(&lock);

Again:

C
counter

doesn't need to be atomic.

The lock makes concurrent access impossible among threads obeying the protocol.

So why did ready need to be atomic?

Because unlike the baton counter, both threads directly access ready concurrently.

Producer:

C
ready = 1;

Consumer:

C
while (ready == 0) {
}

There is no mutex or semaphore protecting those accesses.

If ready is just:

C
int ready;

then we have:

Thread A writes ready
Thread B reads ready
simultaneously

which is a C data race.

So we make:

C
atomic_int ready;

because ready itself is being used as the synchronization mechanism.

That's the difference.

Baton

Synchronization exists separately:

semaphore
   ↓
controls access to
   ↓
ordinary counter
Ready flag

The variable itself participates in synchronization:

atomic ready flag
       ↓
communicates
       ↓
producer → consumer
And data can still be a plain int

This is the subtle part of the acquire/release example:

C
int data = 0;
atomic_int ready = 0;

Producer:

C
data = 42;
atomic_store_explicit(&ready, 1, memory_order_release);

Consumer:

C
while (atomic_load_explicit(&ready, memory_order_acquire) == 0) {
}

printf("%d\n", data);

data does not need to be atomic.

Why?

Because release/acquire establishes:

producer writes data
        ↓
release ready = 1
        ↓
acquire sees ready = 1
        ↓
consumer reads data

So the write to data happens-before the read of data.

There is no concurrent conflicting access to data anymore in the C memory-model sense.

That might sound weird because physically the threads obviously exist simultaneously.

But logically we've proven:

write(data)
must happen before
read(data)

That's enough.

Compare all three

This is probably the cleanest summary.

Unsafe
C
int x = 0;
A writes x
B reads/writes x

nothing orders them

→ data race.

Protected by mutex/semaphore
C
int x = 0;
A ── synchronization ──► B

Only one accesses x at the relevant time.

→ ordinary int is fine.

Atomic object
C
atomic_int x = 0;

Both may access x concurrently, but the language defines how those accesses interact.

→ safe atomic access.

And then there's our publication pattern:

C
int data;
atomic_int ready;

where:

ready

is atomic specifically so that it can establish ordering for the ordinary variable:

data

That's what makes acquire/release powerful.

Where does memory location enter?

Mostly somewhere else.

Remember false sharing:

C
atomic_long a;
atomic_long b;

Whether they were:

8 bytes apart

or:

64 bytes apart

didn't determine whether their increments were correct.

Both versions were correct.

Their locations determined whether the cache-coherence machinery caused awful performance contention.

So:

memory ordering

and:

memory layout

sound annoyingly similar but are very different things.

Memory layout:

Where are the bytes physically/logically arranged?

Relevant to things like cache lines, alignment, false sharing.

Memory ordering:

What ordering between loads/stores is the language and hardware required to make observable?

Relevant to things like acquire/release and happens-before.

That naming collision is probably part of why this suddenly felt contradictory.

Shared mutable data does not inherently need to be atomic. It needs a synchronization strategy that prevents conflicting unordered access.

Sometimes that's a mutex.

Sometimes a semaphore.

Sometimes an atomic object.

Sometimes acquire/release publication.

The invariant determines which mechanism you need.

Yes — and the key thing is that the code you pasted here is actually the spinlock example, not the false-sharing example.

And it works with an ordinary:

C
long counter = 0;

for exactly the same reason the relay worked with a plain long:

The threads are never allowed to access counter concurrently.

The difference is only how that exclusion is enforced.

In the relay:

A gets permit
A touches counter
A hands permit to B
B touches counter
B hands permit to A

So access is explicitly sequenced:

A → B → A → B

In the spinlock:

A and B may both TRY to enter

but only one can successfully acquire:

C
atomic_flag_test_and_set(&lock)

So the actual access becomes:

A owns lock
A touches counter
A releases

or

B owns lock
B touches counter
B releases

The order is nondeterministic, but the overlap is forbidden.

So both give:

no simultaneous conflicting access to counter

and therefore counter itself does not need to be atomic.

The distinction is:

RELAY / SEMAPHORE
A must go, then B must go

SPINLOCK / MUTEX
A or B may go next,
but never both at once

The false-sharing example was different.

There we had things like:

C
atomic_long a = 0;
atomic_long b = 0;

or members like:

C
typedef struct {
    atomic_long a;
    atomic_long b;
} pair;

and each thread directly updated its own atomic:

C
atomic_fetch_add_explicit(&a, 1, memory_order_relaxed);

and:

C
atomic_fetch_add_explicit(&b, 1, memory_order_relaxed);

There was no mutex or semaphore preventing simultaneous access.

Instead:

Thread A modifies a
Thread B modifies b
at the same time

That's safe because a and b are distinct atomic objects.

The problem was performance if they happened to occupy the same cache line.

So:

ordinary counter

      ↑
atomic lock


FALSE SHARING EXAMPLE

atomic a      atomic b
   ↑             ↑
Thread A      Thread B

both may operate simultaneously

So the general rule isn't:

Shared data must be atomic.

It's:

Conflicting accesses must be ordered somehow.

You can order them with:

mutex
spinlock
semaphore
atomic operation
other synchronization

The ordinary long counter is perfectly fine whenever some other mechanism proves that conflicting accesses cannot overlap.

And that is why this example is useful: the atomic_flag is not making counter atomic.

It's making the right to touch counter exclusive.

Exactly.

The plain:

C
long counter = 0;

was safe because this sequence:

C
spin_lock();
counter++;
spin_unlock();

guaranteed that only one thread could perform counter++ at a time.

So the atomicity lived here:

C
atomic_flag_test_and_set(&lock)

not here:

C
counter++;

The atomic flag made the entrance condition indivisible, which created exclusive ownership of the critical section.

So the chain was:

atomic lock acquisition
        ↓
only one thread enters
        ↓
ordinary counter access is serialized
        ↓
plain long is safe

That’s the pattern.

And your false-sharing example was the opposite design choice: we deliberately allowed both threads to operate simultaneously, so the objects they were modifying directly needed atomic semantics.

That gives a very clean split:

Prevent concurrent access
    → protected ordinary data can be fine

Allow concurrent access
    → accesses themselves need appropriate atomic/synchronization semantics

You’re tracking the abstraction boundary correctly now.
